title: Gravitation
summary: Newton's law of universal gravitation, $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$, describes the attraction between any two masses. Surface gravity is $g=GM/R^2$, and for circular orbits gravity supplies the centripetal force, giving $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$.

inverse-square law.in_class: Double the distance ⇒ quarter the force.

concept_sections.heading: Universal gravitation
concept_sections.explanation: Any two masses attract with $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$, directed along the line joining them — the same inverse-square form as the electric force.

concept_sections.heading: The inverse-square law
concept_sections.explanation: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance: doubling $r$ cuts the force to a quarter. This shapes orbits and tides.
math_steps: Twice as far ⇒ one-quarter as strong.

concept_sections.heading: Surface gravity
concept_sections.explanation: A planet's surface gravity is $g=GM/R^2$. Weight $mg$ therefore depends on the planet's mass and radius, not just your mass.

concept_sections.heading: Orbits
concept_sections.explanation: For a circular orbit, gravity is the centripetal force: $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$, so orbital speed is $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$.

concept_sections.heading: Kepler's third law
concept_sections.explanation: Orbital period grows with radius: $T^2\propto r^3$. Combining $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ with $T=2\pi r/v$ gives the relation.

real_world_examples.title: GPS satellites
real_world_examples.scenario: Satellites orbit at a set altitude.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Their orbital speed follows $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$, fixing the orbit's period.

real_world_examples.title: Weight on the Moon
real_world_examples.scenario: You'd weigh less on the Moon.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The Moon's smaller $GM/R^2$ makes $g$ about $1/6$ of Earth's.

real_world_examples.title: Ocean tides
real_world_examples.scenario: The Moon raises tides on Earth.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The inverse-square gravity is slightly stronger on the near side, stretching the oceans.
